verdict: Caution: lend selectively to asset-backed Hosur electronics suppliers with tight monthly discipline; avoid thin-margin assemblers riding the memory-price revenue illusion.
title: Hosur Electronics Manufacturing: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Hosur electronics is a contract-assembly and components trade: you buy chips, boards and displays, convert them into boxes, and sell to an OEM on 60-90 day terms.** Cash is consumed at the input end and released only when the OEM pays, so the working-capital cycle, not the machine, decides survival. Pricing power sits with the OEM; the supplier is a price-taker on components and a cost-taker on labour. **So when a proposal lands, check who the end customer is and what share of turnover is one OEM; if above half, ask for the purchase order and payment history.**

## What has changed now
**The national electronics cycle is strong on paper but the local tax signal is weak.** India IIP for NIC 26 is +19.3% YoY and +13.6% Apr-to-date [D], and electronics exports are +44.0% Apr-to-date in USD [D]. Against that, Tamil Nadu GST collections are -3.2% Apr-to-date versus India +6.1% [D]. **Read this as: the order book may be national, but the cash in Hosur is not yet confirming it.** Peer results show the same split: Dixon revenue +47% to Rs.21,794 crore but profit fell and working capital rose [7], and margins compressed even as revenue surged [6]. **So when a proposal lands, check whether revenue growth is volume or price; if the borrower cannot separate the two, ask for unit volumes month on month.**

## Where the growth is
**The growth is in the supply chain around the Hosur SIPCOT Phase IV EV corridor, a Rs.1,450 crore expansion [1] — but that is a local news report, not a verified order book.** Pursue tier-2 component makers, harness and connector units, and EMS players with a named OEM contract and a PLI-linked customer; the DEAPL rating note shows PLI-backed demand can support 50%+ RoCE and 388% FY2025 revenue growth [10]. **Avoid pure assemblers whose entire margin is a conversion fee and whose revenue is inflated by memory-chip prices rather than units [4].**

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the cycle, not the revenue line.** Take monthly stock and debtor statements, sanction limits against a defined drawing power on receivables, and insist on a charge over current assets. **Take every month: unit volumes, top-customer ageing, and a chip-price note; if volumes are flat while revenue rises, treat it as price inflation, not growth [4].** Cap single-OEM exposure and require personal guarantee where the promoter's net worth is thin.

## Early warning signs
**Watch the gap between revenue and cash.** If debtor days stretch while revenue grows, the borrower is funding the OEM; if GST outflow in the Hosur cluster keeps falling against the national trend [D], the local order book is thinning. **Also watch inventory days: a memory-price spike can sit as expensive stock that will not sell at cost [4].** Rating reports on this city are thin — collect from customer the local cluster data before relying on any Hosur-specific number.
watch: volumes flat while revenue rises -> reprice limit down, ask for chip-price note
ageing beyond 90 days -> freeze fresh disbursement, seek OEM confirmation
two consecutive months below national trend -> shift to cash-collateralised lending
inventory days rising with flat volumes -> demand stock audit, cut drawing power
single OEM above 50% of turnover -> cap exposure, require guarantee
